title: What is inside the Earth?
new_ideas: a true-scale pull from a 12 km hole to the whole planet (the hole becomes a hairline)
ghost pings in the shadow zone that turn solid when the ray is explained (cause shown after effect)
the bell ↔ planet morph used as the film's bookend

lines.text: In 1970, on a frozen peninsula in the far north of Russia, Soviet engineers began to drill a hole straight *down*.

plan.see: Polar night over snowy tundra; a tall drilling rig in a lit shed; two small figures in fur hats at the door.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: tundra horizon comes up from the bottom (1.4 s) | +1.6 the rig inks on, its windows warm | +3.0 snow particles | +4.4 tilt down toward the drill pipe

lines.text: The hole was narrower than a dinner plate, and they kept drilling for almost twenty *years*.

plan.see: A narrow dark shaft descends through rock layers; a counter of years ticks at the side as the drill goes down.
plan.beats: +0.0 ride down the shaft with the drill bit (trail, 5 s) | +1.0 handwritten years 1970→1989 tick on the margin | +4.0 a drill-core plate ★P-04 pinned at the side

lines.text: The deeper they went, the hotter the rock became, until it behaved more like plastic than stone, and the drill could go no *further*.

plan.see: At the bottom, the rock around the bit glows orange and sags; the bit slows and stops.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: red-orange heat rises around the bit (1.6 s) | +2.0 morph: the rock walls sag like wax | +4.0 the bit stops; a puff of steam

lines.text: The hole was meant to reach the boundary beneath the Earth's crust. It never even came *close*.

plan.see: A dashed target line far below the stopped bit; the gap between them is most of the frame.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe down: a dashed line far below appears (1.2 s) | +1.4 a label 'the goal' with a leader line | +2.6 the gap holds

lines.text: Final depth: a little over twelve kilometres. The deepest hole ever *dug*.

plan.see: A red stamp '12,262 m' on the rock at the hole's bottom.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp '12,262 m' (snap) · sfx metal clank −20 | +1.4 hold

lines.text: And yet, on the scale of the whole planet, it is barely a *scratch*.

plan.see: Pull back geometrically: the hole shrinks to an invisible hair on the skin of a whole cutaway Earth.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out ×500 (4 s, geometric) | +2.6 the Earth's cutaway inks on as it arrives | +3.8 label 'the deepest hole' with a leader line to a hairline mark

lines.text: The centre of the Earth lies more than six thousand kilometres below our *feet*.

plan.see: A gold line drops from the surface to the centre of the cutaway; its length dwarfs the hairline hole.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the gold radius traces down (2.4 s, linear) | +2.6 note '6,371 km' writes beside it

lines.text: No one has ever been there. No one ever will. So how do we know what is down *there*?

plan.see: The cutaway's inside is blank paper; question marks of faint ink hover in it.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds close over the inner layers, leaving them blank | +1.6 faint question marks ink on and breathe

lines.text: We cannot dig to it, we cannot see through it, and we cannot send a probe down into *it*.

plan.see: Three tools slide in and fail in turn: a shovel snaps, a lantern dims, a probe melts.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the three tools enter (stagger 0.5 s) | +1.6 snap / dim / melt on each phrase | +4.6 they tear away

lines.text: Yet today we can draw the inside of the Earth layer by layer: a thin crust, a thick mantle, an ocean of liquid metal… and at the centre, a solid ball as hot as the surface of the *Sun*.

plan.see: The blank cutaway fills with its layers one by one, painted as in an old atlas; at the centre a small gold-white ball.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core paint in from the outside (1.2 s each) | +5.0 the inner ball blooms white-gold

lines.text: That picture came from four clues — and the most important of them came from the planet's worst *moments*.

plan.see: A small crack appears on the surface of the drawn Earth; rings of shock spread from it.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill marks a point on the crust | +1.6 a crack and a ripple spread from it (1.4 s)

lines.text: Our first clue is a *weight*.

plan.see: Clue tag 1/4; title 'Clue I · The Weight of the World' writes on above a brass weight.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 1 | +0.2 text title | +1.0 a brass weight drops into frame

lines.text: In 1798, in an outbuilding at his house in London, Henry Cavendish set out to weigh the *world*.

plan.see: A plain wooden outbuilding in a London garden; inside, a long wooden case; the shy, old-fashioned gentleman outside it.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the garden and the outbuilding (1.6 s) | +1.8 Cavendish (Person, 18th-c. coat, grey wig) inks on | +3.4 cabinet card ★P-08

lines.text: Not with a scale — you cannot put a planet on a scale — but by measuring how strongly lead attracts *lead*.

plan.see: An empty shop scale with the Earth too big for it; beside it, two lead balls with faint gold lines of pull between them.
plan.beats: +0.0 ink-on: a shop scale; the Earth hovers over it, far too big (1.2 s) | +1.8 morph: the scale becomes two lead balls with pull lines

lines.text: Inside, he hung a rod from a fine wire, with a small lead ball at each end, and set two heavy lead balls close *beside* them.

plan.see: A window into the case: the torsion rod on its wire, two small balls, two big balls near them.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris into the case (1.2 s) | +1.4 the rod and small balls ink on | +3.0 the large balls swing in close

lines.text: To keep his own warmth from stirring the air, he watched from outside, through a *telescope*.

plan.see: Outside the wall: Cavendish at a small telescope poking through it; we see what he sees — a scale and a pointer.
plan.beats: +0.0 match: the iris circle becomes his telescope's view | +1.4 he leans to the eyepiece (pose look)

lines.text: The heavy balls pulled on the small ones — gently, almost nothing — and the rod turned by a *hair*.

plan.see: In the telescope's view, the pointer creeps along the ivory scale by one tiny division.
plan.beats: +0.0 push into the view | +1.0 thin gold lines of pull grow between the balls | +2.6 the pointer creeps one division (3 s, linear)

lines.text: From that tiny turn, he worked out how strongly the whole Earth pulls… and so how heavy it must *be*.

plan.see: Pull back: the whole Earth sits in the pan of a great brass balance.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out from the pointer to the Earth (2 s) | +2.0 a brass balance inks on under it

lines.text: The answer was strange. On average, the Earth was about five and a half times as dense as *water*.

plan.see: His real paper ★D-03 slides in; '5.48' circled in red.
plan.beats: +0.0 ★D-03 slides in (1.0 s) | +1.6 red circle round 5.48

lines.text: But the rocks under our feet are only about half that *dense*.

plan.see: A chunk of granite on one pan, the same size of 'Earth' on the other — the Earth side sinks hard.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: a granite chunk onto the left pan | +1.0 the balance tips heavily to the Earth side (back)

lines.text: So something deep inside had to be far heavier than *rock*.

plan.see: Inside the cutaway, the centre darkens and glows: a heavy heart pulls the balance down.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris into the cutaway | +1.4 the centre darkens to iron grey with a warm rim

lines.text: In the 1890s, the German scientist Emil Wiechert suggested what it was: iron, like the iron meteorites that fall from the *sky*.

plan.see: An iron meteorite streaks down and lands beside Wiechert; its crystal pattern morphs into the Earth's core.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: a meteorite falls (trail, 1.4 s) | +1.6 Wiechert (Person) beside it | +3.0 morph: its etched pattern becomes the core

lines.text: A heavy heart of metal. But it was only a guess. Nobody could look *inside*.

plan.see: The core drawing tears into a blank again, with a pencilled '?'.
plan.beats: +0.0 tear-away over the core (1.0 s) | +1.2 a pencilled '?' writes on

lines.text: Clue two: the planet *rings*.

plan.see: Clue tag 2/4; a bronze bell is struck; its rings of sound fill the page.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 2 | +0.2 title 'Clue II · The Ringing Planet' | +1.0 the bell is struck; ripples

lines.text: When a great earthquake strikes, it sends waves through the whole Earth, the way a struck bell sends sound through its *metal*.

plan.see: The bell morphs into the Earth; from a quake point, rays of waves fan through the inside in curves.
plan.beats: +0.0 morph: bell → globe cutaway (1.6 s) | +1.8 grow: curved ray paths fan through the mantle (trail ×7, stagger)

lines.text: Some waves push and squeeze, like sound. Others shake from side to side, like a rope being *flicked*.

plan.see: Two small panels: a coiled spring squeezing along (P) and a rope whipping side to side (S).
plan.beats: +0.0 slide in the two panels | +0.8 the spring pulses (loop) | +2.4 the rope flicks (loop) | +3.6 labels 'P' and 'S' (label style)

lines.text: And their speed depends on what they pass through: faster in hard, dense rock, slower in softer or hotter *material*.

plan.see: Two lanes of rock, one hard and dark, one soft and warm; the same pulse runs fast in one, slower in the other.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe: two lanes of rock (1.0 s) | +1.2 pulses race in both (trail) | +3.0 the hard-rock pulse wins

lines.text: By 1900, observatories around the world had seismographs: needles that drew every tremor on a turning drum of *paper*.

plan.see: A brass seismograph with a heavy pendulum and a smoked-paper drum turning; its needle scratches a line; real footage ★V-01 in an old screen beside it.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the instrument comes up from below (1.4 s) | +1.6 the drum turns; the needle draws a calm line | +3.6 ★V-01 plays in an OldScreen frame

lines.text: Each earthquake became a message, written in ink in many cities at once — but only for someone who could *read* it.

plan.see: Whip across a grid of small drums in different cities; the same jagged signal appears on each, slightly later the farther it is.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: six drums in a grid (0.3 s each) | +2.0 the same signature scratches across them in sequence

lines.text: In 1897, a huge earthquake shook Assam, in north-eastern *India*.

plan.see: A window onto green hills of Assam; buildings shake and crack; a real damage photo ★P-09 pinned at the corner.
plan.beats: +0.0 window opens on India on the globe (1.2 s) | +1.4 crane over the hills | +2.4 tremble: houses crack | +4.0 ★P-09 pinned

lines.text: Richard Dixon Oldham, of the Geological Survey of India, collected the records of its waves from stations around the *globe*.

plan.see: Oldham at a desk piled with paper records and envelopes from far cities; his real portrait as a small plate.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the desk enters from left | +1.6 envelopes drop in, each stamped with a city | +3.4 ★P-05 plate

lines.text: Waves that crossed near the surface arrived on time. But waves that dived deep through the middle of the Earth came in *late*.

plan.see: Back in the cutaway: two pulses race — a shallow one arrives; a deep one, through the centre, lags behind its expected mark.
plan.beats: +0.0 two pulses leave the quake (trail) | +2.2 the shallow one hits its mark on time (ping) | +3.8 the deep one arrives late; a red gap between 'expected' and 'arrived'

lines.text: Like runners who hit mud in the middle of a race, they had passed through something *different*.

plan.see: Tiny runners on a track; in the middle stretch the track turns to mud and they slow down.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: a track crosses the frame | +1.0 runners enter | +2.4 the middle turns to mud; they slow

lines.text: Something in the centre was *slowing* them down.

plan.see: The centre of the cutaway darkens into a distinct ball; the deep ray bends as it enters it.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: the central ball emerges (1.2 s) | +1.6 the ray bends at its edge

lines.text: In 1906, Oldham published his conclusion: the Earth has a *core*.

plan.see: His real paper ★D-02 slides in; a red stamp 'CORE' beside it.
plan.beats: +0.0 ★D-02 slides in | +1.4 stamp 'Core, 1906'

lines.text: Clue three: a wave that goes *missing*.

plan.see: Clue tag 3/4; title 'Clue III · The Missing Wave'.
plan.beats: +0.0 page-turn | +0.4 clue tag 3 | +0.6 title

lines.text: In 1909, an earthquake struck near Zagreb, and the Croatian scientist Andrija Mohorovičić noticed that its waves arrived *twice*.

plan.see: Zagreb observatory; Mohorovičić over a seismogram with two separate bursts marked.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the observatory room (1.4 s) | +1.6 Mohorovičić (Person) | +3.0 two bursts on the record are circled | +4.4 ★P-06

lines.text: Some came straight through the crust. But others dived a little deeper, into faster rock, and raced *ahead*.

plan.see: A slab of crust in section: one ray travels along the top; another dips into the faster layer below, runs, and climbs back — overtaking it.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the slab section | +1.0 two rays race (trail) | +3.0 the deeper one overtakes

lines.text: He had found the bottom of the crust — only a few tens of kilometres down. Today it carries his name: the *Moho*.

plan.see: A gold boundary line inks across the slab; a handwritten label 'Moho'.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill draws the boundary (1.6 s) | +2.0 note 'the Moho'

lines.text: Beneath that thin skin lies the mantle: hot, solid rock that slowly creeps, like very thick *honey*.

plan.see: Below the Moho line, the mantle paints in; slow loops of motion drift through it like honey stirred by a spoon.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the mantle layer below the gold line (1.4 s) | +1.6 morph: slow convection loops (trail loops, 4 s)

lines.text: In 1914, Beno Gutenberg measured where the core begins: about two thousand nine hundred kilometres *down*.

plan.see: Pull back to the whole cutaway; a ring marks the top of the core; Gutenberg's small portrait beside it.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out from the slab to the planet (2 s) | +2.0 a ring around the core boundary | +3.0 figure '2,900 km' | +3.8 ★P-07

lines.text: Then seismologists noticed something stranger. The side-to-side waves never came through the core at *all*.

plan.see: Shake-waves (drawn as rope-like zigzags) travel down, reach the core's edge, and stop dead.
plan.beats: +0.0 zigzag rays travel (trail) | +2.4 they hit the core boundary and vanish (a small puff)

lines.text: Those waves can travel through solids, but never through *liquids*.

plan.see: Two glass tanks: a block of jelly carries a side-to-side wobble; a tank of water does not.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds reveal the two tanks | +1.0 the jelly wobbles across | +2.4 in the water, the wobble dies at once

lines.text: So the core was liquid: an ocean of molten iron, thousands of kilometres *deep*.

plan.see: The core blooms into molten orange; slow currents swirl in it.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: the core turns molten (1.6 s) | +1.8 swirling currents (trail loops)

lines.text: And a liquid core, bending the waves like a lens, casts a *shadow*.

plan.see: Rays from the quake bend through the core and leave a dark band on the far side of the planet.
plan.beats: +0.0 rays bend through the core (trail ×9) | +2.4 a dark ring of shadow darkens on the far surface

lines.text: Waves bend whenever they enter a new material, just as a straw seems to bend in a glass of *water*.

plan.see: A glass of water with a straw that appears broken at the surface.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the glass comes up (1.0 s) | +1.2 the straw bends visibly at the waterline (morph 1 s)

lines.text: On the far side of the planet from an earthquake, there is a ring where the main waves should never *arrive*.

plan.see: The globe turns to show the shadow ring; a label marks it.
plan.beats: +0.0 orbit: lon +40° (3 s) | +1.4 label 'shadow zone' with a leader line

lines.text: But they did. Faint, ghostly ones. And nobody could explain *them*.

plan.see: Inside the shadow ring, a few pale pings flicker where nothing should be.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris into the shadow ring | +1.0 three ghost pings blink (low alpha)

lines.text: Clue four: a ghost in the *shadow*.

plan.see: Clue tag 4/4; title 'Clue IV · A Ghost in the Shadow'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 4 | +0.2 title

lines.text: In Copenhagen, Inge Lehmann led the seismology department of Denmark's Geodetic *Institute*.

plan.see: A 1930s office in Copenhagen: tall window, piles of records; Inge Lehmann at the desk; her real portrait as a cabinet card.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the office (1.6 s) | +1.8 Lehmann (Person, 1930s dress, hair in a bun, round spectacles) | +3.4 ★P-01 cabinet card

lines.text: She was a patient, exact reader of squiggles on *paper*.

plan.see: A loupe glides along a real seismogram ★D-05; the squiggles enlarge under the glass.
plan.beats: +0.0 Loupe over ★D-05 (focus moves left→right, 3 s)

lines.text: In 1929, a strong earthquake struck Buller, on New Zealand's South Island — on the far side of the world from *Europe*.

plan.see: The globe turns to New Zealand; a ripple bursts there; a window shows a landslide; a real photo ★P-10 pinned.
plan.beats: +0.0 orbit to New Zealand (2 s) | +1.6 ripple at Buller | +2.4 window: the landslide | +4.0 ★P-10

lines.text: Its waves crossed the whole planet, and stations in Europe recorded *them*.

plan.see: Rays from New Zealand cross through the cutaway to small station pins in Europe.
plan.beats: +0.0 ride along a ray through the planet (3 s) | +2.6 pins light up: Copenhagen and others

lines.text: Lehmann studied the records. In the shadow zone, where nothing should arrive, faint waves *had* arrived.

plan.see: Her loupe finds a tiny bump on a record where the line should be flat.
plan.beats: +0.0 Loupe stops over a small bump | +1.4 red circle

lines.text: Others called them noise, or waves that had bent around the edge of the *core*.

plan.see: Letters from colleagues slide over the desk with sketched explanations; one shows a ray bending round the core's rim.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: three letters overlap | +1.4 the top one shows the bending sketch

lines.text: Lehmann tried another idea. Was the liquid core really liquid all the way *through*?

plan.see: She draws, in pencil, a small circle inside the core.
plan.beats: +0.0 Lehmann's pencil draws a circle inside the core (quill, 1.6 s)

lines.text: Suppose a smaller, solid ball sat at the very centre. It would catch those waves, bend them, and throw them into the shadow — exactly where they were *seen*.

plan.see: A ray dives into the small inner ball, bends sharply, and lands inside the shadow ring — on the ghost ping.
plan.beats: +0.0 ride with the ray into the core (2 s) | +2.2 it refracts at the inner ball | +3.6 it lands on the ghost ping, which turns solid

lines.text: She worked it out with pencil and paper, and kept her data on cards in old oatmeal *boxes*.

plan.see: Cardboard cereal boxes full of index cards; one card lifts out; a real card/record ★P-02 revealed.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: two boxes land on the desk | +1.2 a card lifts (lift) | +2.4 real-reveal ★P-02

lines.text: In 1936, at forty-eight, she published it. The title of her paper was a single symbol: *P-prime*.

plan.see: The real paper ★D-01 with its tiny title 'P′'; the title circled; the gold figure 'P′'.
plan.beats: +0.0 ★D-01 slides in | +1.4 circle round 'P′' | +2.4 figure 'P′' in gold

lines.text: Her idea was so simple it was easy to doubt. But within a few years, the leading seismologists had *accepted* it.

plan.see: The sceptical letters flip over one by one; on their backs: short notes of agreement.
plan.beats: +0.0 flip: the letters turn (stagger 0.5 s) | +2.0 the last one: a handwritten 'agreed'

lines.text: The Earth had an inner *core*.

plan.see: The inner ball at the centre of the cutaway blooms white-gold.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out to the whole planet | +1.0 bloom of the inner core

lines.text: Today we know that inner core is a ball of solid iron and nickel, about two thousand four hundred kilometres *across*.

plan.see: The inner core drawn large, with crystalline texture; a small Moon floats beside it for scale.
plan.beats: +0.0 push into the inner core | +1.6 a Moon inks on beside it for scale | +3.4 label 'about the size of the Moon'

lines.text: It is about as hot as the surface of the Sun — and yet it is *solid*, squeezed by the weight of the whole planet above it.

plan.see: Inward arrows press on the white-hot ball from every side; it stays solid, glowing.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: the Sun's surface flashes beside it for comparison | +1.8 collapse: arrows press in from all around

lines.text: Its heat is left over partly from the planet's birth, and partly made by radioactive atoms still decaying deep *inside*.

plan.see: Tiny sparks glint here and there through the mantle and core like distant fires.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: sparks light up through the interior (2 s)

lines.text: Around it, the liquid iron of the outer core keeps moving, and that motion makes the Earth's magnetic *field*.

plan.see: Currents swirl in the outer core; magnetic field lines rise out of the planet and loop into space.
plan.beats: +0.0 orbit slowly | +1.0 currents swirl | +2.4 field lines grow out of the poles (trail ×8)

lines.text: The same field that turns a compass needle, and shields our air from the wind of the *Sun*.

plan.see: A compass needle swings to north on a hand; pull back: particles from the Sun stream past and are turned aside by the field lines.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the compass | +1.2 pull back to space | +2.4 photons stream from left and deflect around the field

lines.text: The deepest place on our planet was found not by going there… but by *listening*.

plan.see: The planet shrinks into the bronze bell of clue two; it rings softly.
plan.beats: +0.0 match: Earth → bell (1.4 s) | +1.6 a soft ripple

lines.text: And by a woman who kept working for decades after that discovery, and lived to be one hundred and *four*.

plan.see: The cabinet card of young Lehmann flips; on its back, a photo of her very old, smiling.
plan.beats: +0.0 flip: the card turns (flipY 0→180, back) | +1.6 the older portrait from ★P-01 set | +3.0 plate '1888–1993'

lines.text: So — how do we know what is inside the *Earth*?

plan.see: The cutaway Earth alone in space again.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out | +1.0 bloom

lines.text: Its weight told us the middle is heavy. Its echoes told us there is a *core*.

plan.see: Around the planet, small medallions return: the balance, the seismograph drum.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: two medallions on each phrase (1.0 s apart)

lines.text: A missing wave told us the core is liquid. And a ghost in the shadow told us that, at the very centre, it turns solid *again*.

plan.see: Two more medallions: the jelly tank, the oatmeal box; all four slide into the layers of the cutaway, which light in order.
plan.beats: +0.0 two medallions | +2.4 collapse: all four slide into the layers | +4.6 the inner core glows last

lines.text: Every big earthquake is still a lesson. Thousands of seismometers listen, and each wave adds a little more to the *map*.

plan.see: Crane over the globe: thousands of tiny station pins light up across continents as a ripple passes.
plan.beats: +0.0 crane over the planet | +1.0 pins light in a wave following a ripple (3 s)

lines.text: The same trick now works on other worlds: a quake felt on another planet can reveal its heart *too*.

plan.see: Whip to a small red planet; a ripple crosses it; its own core shows faintly through a cutaway.
plan.beats: +0.0 whip to a red planet (0.6 s, expo) | +0.8 a ripple crosses it | +2.0 its cutaway core inks on

lines.text: We will never stand at the centre of the *Earth*.

plan.see: The Kola rig again, tiny on the white tundra.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe: back to the tundra and the rig (1.4 s)

lines.text: But we know its shape, its heat and its metal — because the planet keeps talking, and someone learned to *listen*.

plan.see: From the rig, pull down through the snow into the drawn cutaway one last time; it rings softly; the brand end card follows.
plan.beats: +0.0 pull down through the ground into the cutaway (3 s) | +2.4 a final soft ripple | +4.0 end card
